questions.topic: Particle Dynamics - 2D Motion under Constant Forces (Velocity)
questions.q: Two forces $\vec{F}_1 = (-6\hat{i} - 4\hat{j})\text{ N}$ and $\vec{F}_2 = (-3\hat{i} + 7\hat{j})\text{ N}$ act on a particle of mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$ initially at rest at the origin. Determine the velocity vector $\vec{v}$ of the particle after a time interval $t = 10\text{ s}$.
questions.hint: First calculate the net force $\vec{F} = \vec{F}_1 + \vec{F}_2$, then find the acceleration $\vec{a} = \frac{\vec{F}}{m}$, and finally the velocity vector using $\vec{v} = \vec{a} \cdot t$.
explanations: Correct! The net force is $\vec{F} = (-6 - 3)\hat{i} + (-4 + 7)\hat{j} = -9\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}\text{ N}$. The acceleration is $\vec{a} = \frac{\vec{F}}{2} = -4.5\hat{i} + 1.5\hat{j}\text{ m/s}^2$. Multiplying by $t = 10\text{ s}$ gives $\vec{v} = \vec{a} \cdot t = -45\hat{i} + 15\hat{j}\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. This result is obtained by forgetting to divide the total force by the mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$.
Incorrect. This is the acceleration $\vec{a}$ expressed in $\text{m/s}^2$, not the velocity at time $t = 10\text{ s}$.
Incorrect. Calculation error in adding force components or applying time.

questions.topic: Particle Dynamics - 2D Motion under Constant Forces (Position)
questions.q: Referring to the previous problem (forces $\vec{F}_1 = (-6\hat{i} - 4\hat{j})\text{ N}$ and $\vec{F}_2 = (-3\hat{i} + 7\hat{j})\text{ N}$, mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$), determine the position vector $\vec{s}$ of the particle at $t = 10\text{ s}$, knowing that it starts from rest at the origin.
questions.hint: Since acceleration $\vec{a}$ is constant and the particle starts from rest at the origin, the vector equation of motion is $\vec{s} = \frac{1}{2} \vec{a} t^2$.
explanations: Correct! Since acceleration is $\vec{a} = (-4.5\hat{i} + 1.5\hat{j})\text{ m/s}^2$, applying $\vec{s} = \frac{1}{2} \vec{a} t^2$ with $t^2 = 100\text{ s}^2$ gives $\vec{s} = 0.5 \cdot (-4.5\hat{i} + 1.5\hat{j}) \cdot 100 = -225\hat{i} + 75\hat{j}\text{ m}$.
Incorrect. Forgot the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ in the position formula for uniformly accelerated motion.
Incorrect. This value is obtained if $t$ is used instead of $t^2$ in the equation of motion.
Incorrect. Divided further by two due to an error in calculating acceleration or time.

questions.topic: Dynamics with Friction - Horizontal Plane and Inclined Pull
questions.q: A passenger at the airport pulls her suitcase of mass $m = 20\text{ kg}$ at constant speed, applying a force $F = 35\text{ N}$ to a strap inclined at an angle $\theta = 30^\circ$ relative to the horizontal. Determine the coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_d$ between the suitcase and the floor (assuming $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$).
questions.hint: Since the motion is at constant speed, the horizontal force balances friction: $F \cos\theta = F_d = \mu_d \cdot N$. The normal force is $N = m \cdot g - F \sin\theta$.
explanations: Correct! The horizontal component is $F_x = 35 \cdot \cos(30^\circ) \approx 30.31\text{ N}$. The vertical normal force is $N = m g - F \sin(30^\circ) = 20 \cdot 9.81 - 35 \cdot 0.5 = 196.2 - 17.5 = 178.7\text{ N}$. Consequently, $\mu_d = \frac{F_x}{N} = \frac{30.31}{178.7} \approx 0.17$.
Incorrect. $0.15$ is obtained by not subtracting the vertical component of tension $F \sin\theta$ from weight $m \cdot g$.
Incorrect. Error in swapping trigonometric functions sine and cosine.
Incorrect. Results from a calculation error in weight or in the vertical equilibrium equation.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics - Flat Curve with Friction
questions.q: A car of mass $m = 1500\text{ kg}$ moving on a flat horizontal road negotiates a curve of radius $R = 35\text{ m}$. If the coefficient of friction between the tires and the asphalt is $\mu = 0.573$, what is the maximum speed $v_{max}$ at which the car can round the curve without skidding (assuming $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$)?
questions.hint: The maximum friction force provides the necessary centripetal force to turn: $F_a = F_c \implies \mu m g = m \frac{v_{max}^2}{R}$, from which $v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu g R}$.
explanations: Correct! Equating maximum friction to centripetal force yields $v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu g R} = \sqrt{0.573 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 35} = \sqrt{196.74} \approx 14.03\text{ m/s}$. Converting to $\text{km/h}$ ($14.03 \cdot 3.6$) yields $\approx 50.5\text{ km/h}$.
Incorrect. $196.74$ is the value of $v_{max}^2$, forgetting to take the square root.
Incorrect. Error in the value used for gravitational acceleration $g$ or in the product inside the square root.
Incorrect. Result derived from an incorrect estimate not based on the centripetal equilibrium formula.

questions.topic: Inclined Plane Dynamics - Static Equilibrium Condition
questions.q: A snowstorm causes fresh snow to accumulate on a ski slope. If the coefficient of static friction between the fresh snow and the underlying layer is $\mu = 0.46$, what is the maximum angle of inclination $\theta$ of the slope such that the fresh snow layer does not slide off?
questions.hint: At the critical angle of traction, the component of gravity parallel to the plane equals the maximum static friction force: $m g \sin\theta = \mu m g \cos\theta \implies \tan\theta = \mu$.
explanations: Correct! From the equilibrium condition along the slope, we get $\tan\theta = \mu = 0.46$. Calculating arctangent: $\theta = \arctan(0.46) \approx 24.7^\circ \approx 25^\circ$.
Incorrect. Result derived from incorrectly using arcsine instead of arctangent.
Incorrect. Result derived from incorrectly using arccosine.
Incorrect. $30^\circ$ is a standard inclination angle but does not correspond to $\tan\theta = 0.46$.

questions.topic: Simple Harmonic Motion - Maximum Velocity
questions.q: A mass $m = 200\text{ g}$ oscillates horizontally without friction on the end of a spring with spring constant $k = 7.0\text{ N/m}$. If the mass is displaced by $A = 5.0\text{ cm}$ from the equilibrium position and released, calculate its maximum speed $v_{max}$.
questions.hint: The angular frequency of the oscillator is $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$. The maximum speed is reached when passing through the equilibrium position and is given by $v_{max} = A \cdot \omega$. Remember to convert mass to $\text{kg}$ and displacement to $\text{m}$.
explanations: Correct! Converting data: $m = 0.2\text{ kg}$ and $A = 0.05\text{ m}$. The angular frequency is $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{7.0}{0.2}} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.916\text{ rad/s}$. The maximum speed is $v_{max} = A \cdot \omega = 0.05 \cdot 5.916 \approx 0.295\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. Result doubled due to an error in calculating amplitude or angular frequency.
Incorrect. $1.75\text{ m/s}^2$ is the value of maximum acceleration $a_{max}$, not speed.
Incorrect. Error in unit conversion or in taking the square root.
Incorrect. Results from forgetting to correctly square or take the square root of the ratio $k/m$.

questions.topic: Simple Harmonic Motion - Maximum Acceleration
questions.q: Using the data from the previous problem ($m = 200\text{ g}$, $k = 7.0\text{ N/m}$, $A = 5.0\text{ cm}$), calculate the maximum acceleration $a_{max}$ of the oscillating mass.
questions.hint: The maximum acceleration in simple harmonic motion occurs at the extremes of oscillation and is related to amplitude by the formula $a_{max} = A \cdot \omega^2 = A \cdot \frac{k}{m}$.
explanations: Correct! Since $\omega^2 = \frac{k}{m} = \frac{7.0}{0.2} = 35\text{ rad}^2/\text{s}^2$, maximum acceleration is obtained as $a_{max} = A \cdot \omega^2 = 0.05 \cdot 35 = 1.75\text{ m/s}^2$.
Incorrect. $3.50\text{ m/s}^2$ is obtained by not dividing correctly by the amplitude factor or by multiplying by two.
Incorrect. $0.295\text{ m/s}^2$ is the value of maximum speed expressed in $\text{m/s}$.
Incorrect. Halving error in the final calculation.
Incorrect. Corresponds to the value of spring constant $k$ alone without considering mass and amplitude.

questions.topic: Simple Harmonic Motion - Oscillation Frequency
questions.q: Determine the oscillation frequency $\nu$ of the mass in the spring-mass system ($m = 200\text{ g}$, $k = 7.0\text{ N/m}$).
questions.hint: The frequency $\nu$ is related to angular frequency $\omega$ by $\nu = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$.
explanations: Correct! First calculating angular frequency $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{7.0}{0.2}} \approx 5.916\text{ rad/s}$, we get frequency $\nu = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{5.916}{2\pi} \approx 0.942\text{ Hz}$.
Incorrect. $5.92\text{ rad/s}$ is angular frequency $\omega$, not frequency in Hertz $\nu$.
Incorrect. $1.06\text{ s}$ represents the oscillation period $T = \frac{1}{\nu}$, not frequency.
Incorrect. Result obtained by dividing by $4\pi$ instead of $2\pi$.
Incorrect. Result obtained by dividing $\omega$ by $\pi$ only, instead of $2\pi$.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics - Slipping Condition on a Turntable
questions.q: An object of mass $M = 1\text{ kg}$ rests on a horizontal turntable at a distance $R = 6\text{ m}$ from the center. The coefficient of static friction is $\mu = 1.2$. If the turntable starts rotating from rest with constant angular acceleration $\alpha = 1\text{ rad/s}^2$, calculate the time $t$ at which the mass starts slipping along the platform (assuming $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$).
questions.hint: Calculate maximum static friction force $F_a = \mu M g$ and tangential force $F_t = M \alpha R$. Equating the sum of force components needed to friction force $F_t + F_c = F_a$ with $F_c = M \omega^2 R$, determine $\omega$ and then time $t = \frac{\omega}{\alpha}$.
explanations: Correct! Maximum friction force is $F_a = 1.2 \cdot 1 \cdot 9.81 = 11.77\text{ N}$. Tangential force is $F_t = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 6 = 6\text{ N}$. Applying balance equation $F_t + F_c = F_a \implies 6 + 1 \cdot \omega^2 \cdot 6 = 11.77 \implies 6 \omega^2 = 5.77 \implies \omega = \sqrt{\frac{5.77}{6}} \approx 0.98\text{ rad/s}$. Since $\alpha = 1\text{ rad/s}^2$, slipping time is $t = \frac{\omega}{\alpha} \approx 0.98\text{ s} \approx 1.0\text{ s}$.
Incorrect. $2.00\text{ s}$ comes from an incorrect estimate doubling the limiting slip time.
Incorrect. $0.50\text{ s}$ is obtained from an error in calculating friction force or square root.
Incorrect. $1.96\text{ s}$ is obtained by neglecting the tangential force component $F_t$.
Incorrect. Result due to errors in converting angular acceleration.

questions.topic: Static Equilibrium - Tension in the First Cable (Example 1)
questions.q: A traffic light of weight $W = 100\text{ N}$ is suspended by a knot of three cables. Cable 3 hangs vertically supporting the traffic light ($T_3 = 100\text{ N}$), while cables 1 and 2 form angles of $37^\circ$ and $53^\circ$ respectively with the upper horizontal support. What is the tension $T_1$ in the first cable?
questions.hint: Decompose forces along $x$ and $y$ axes: $\sum F_x = T_2 \cos 53^\circ - T_1 \cos 37^\circ = 0$ and $\sum F_y = T_1 \sin 37^\circ + T_2 \sin 53^\circ - 100 = 0$. Express $T_2$ in terms of $T_1$ and substitute.
explanations: Correct! From the first equation along $x$, we have $T_2 = T_1 \frac{\cos 37^\circ}{\cos 53^\circ} \approx 1.33 T_1$. Substituting into the second vertical equation: $T_1 \sin 37^\circ + 1.33 T_1 \sin 53^\circ = 100 \implies T_1 (0.602 + 1.062) = 100 \implies T_1 = 60.0\text{ N}$.
Incorrect. $79.8\text{ N}$ is tension $T_2$ in the second cable.
Incorrect. $100\text{ N}$ is the total weight of the traffic light $W$, supported by vertical cable $T_3$.
Incorrect. $1.33$ is the ratio of the two tensions ($T_2 / T_1$), not force in Newtons.

questions.topic: Static Equilibrium - Tension in the Second Cable (Example 1)
questions.q: With reference to the equilibrium system of the traffic light ($W = 100\text{ N}$, angles $37^\circ$ and $53^\circ$), what is the value of tension $T_2$ in the second cable making an angle of $53^\circ$ with the horizontal?
questions.hint: Use the relationship between tensions $T_2 = T_1 \frac{\cos 37^\circ}{\cos 53^\circ} \approx 1.33 T_1$ and the previously calculated value $T_1 = 60.0\text{ N}$.
explanations: Correct! Having found $T_1 = 60.0\text{ N}$, $T_2 = 1.33 \cdot 60.0\text{ N} = 79.8\text{ N}$.
Incorrect. $60.0\text{ N}$ is tension $T_1$ in the first cable.
Incorrect. $100\text{ N}$ is the tension in vertical cable $T_3$.
Incorrect. Error in calculating trigonometric ratio.

questions.topic: Static Equilibrium Theory - Symmetry of Tensions
questions.q: Consider an object of weight $W$ supported by two upper inclined attachment cables. Under what condition are the tensions in the two inclined attachment cables exactly equal ($T_1 = T_2$)?
questions.hint: Observe horizontal equilibrium equation $T_2 \cos\theta_2 - T_1 \cos\theta_1 = 0$. In what case do the two components balance with identical tensions?
options: When the two cables form equal angles relative to the horizontal support
When the angle of one cable is exactly twice the other
Tensions are always equal regardless of the angles
When the lengths of the two cables are different
explanations: Correct! For $T_1 = T_2$, horizontal equilibrium $T_1 \cos\theta_1 = T_2 \cos\theta_2$ requires $\cos\theta_1 = \cos\theta_2$, meaning the angles made by the cables with the horizontal beam must be identical.
Incorrect. If angles are different, cosines differ and thus tensions must differ to ensure horizontal balance.
Incorrect. Tensions vary as structure geometry and angles change.
Incorrect. Cable length does not directly affect force equilibrium; angular inclination is what matters.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics - Maximum Rotational Speed (Example 2)
questions.q: An object of mass $m = 0.500\text{ kg}$ is tied to a string of length $r = 1.50\text{ m}$ and rotates in a horizontal circle. If the string can withstand a maximum tension $T_{max} = 50.0\text{ N}$ before breaking, what is the maximum speed $v_{max}$ the object can reach?
questions.hint: Equate maximum tension to centripetal force: $T_{max} = m \frac{v_{max}^2}{r}$, from which $v_{max} = \sqrt{\frac{T_{max} \cdot r}{m}}$.
explanations: Correct! Applying the formula $v_{max} = \sqrt{\frac{T_{max} \cdot r}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{50.0 \cdot 1.50}{0.500}} = \sqrt{150} \approx 12.247\text{ m/s} \approx 12.2\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $150$ is the value of $v^2$ before taking the square root.
Incorrect. Calculation error in placing mass in the denominator.
Incorrect. Multiplication/division error in algebraic steps.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Theory - Origin of Centripetal Force
questions.q: A body of mass $m$ moves in uniform circular motion on a smooth horizontal plane attached to a string. Which force provides the centripetal acceleration required to constrain the body to the circular path?
questions.hint: Consider the direction of the force needed to continuously curve toward the center of the circle.
options: The tension $T$ exerted by the string on the body
The weight force of the body $m \cdot g$
The normal force of the plane directed upward
explanations: Correct! Tension $T$ directed toward the center along the trajectory radius provides the only net radial force and constitutes the centripetal force responsible for changing the direction of velocity.
Incorrect. Weight acts vertically and is balanced by normal force from the horizontal plane.
Incorrect. Normal force balances gravity vertically and does not act in the radial direction.
Incorrect. Tangential inertial force is not radially directed toward the center.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Theory - Relationship between Tension and Velocity
questions.q: In horizontal circular motion with a string of constant length $r$, how does the tension $T$ exerted by the string vary as the tangential speed $v$ of the body increases?
questions.hint: Recall Newton's Second Law for the radial direction: $T = m \cdot a_c = m \frac{v^2}{r}$.
options: Tension $T$ increases with the square of speed ($T \propto v^2$)
Tension $T$ increases directly proportional to speed ($T \propto v$)
Tension $T$ remains constant regardless of speed
explanations: Correct! Since centripetal force is proportional to $v^2$, tension $T = m \frac{v^2}{r}$ grows quadratically as speed $v$ increases. Doubling speed quadruples tension.
Incorrect. Speed is squared in the centripetal acceleration expression, not linear.
Incorrect. To make a body rotate faster requires a larger centripetal force, not smaller.
Incorrect. Tension increases significantly when rotation frequency or speed increases.

questions.topic: Universal Gravitation - Earth-Moon Gravitational Attraction
questions.q: Determine the gravitational attraction force between the Earth and the Moon knowing that the average Earth-Moon distance is $d = 384000\text{ km}$ ($M_T = 5.972 \cdot 10^{24}\text{ kg}$, $M_L = 7.34 \cdot 10^{22}\text{ kg}$, $G = 6.674 \cdot 10^{-11}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$).
questions.hint: Apply Newton's law of universal gravitation: $F = G \frac{M_T \cdot M_L}{d^2}$. Remember to convert distance to meters first ($384000\text{ km} = 3.84 \cdot 10^8\text{ m}$).
explanations: Correct! Expressing distance in meters $d = 3.84 \cdot 10^8\text{ m}$, we calculate $F = (6.674 \cdot 10^{-11}) \cdot \frac{(5.972 \cdot 10^{24}) \cdot (7.34 \cdot 10^{22})}{(3.84 \cdot 10^8)^2} \approx 1.98 \cdot 10^{20}\text{ N}$.
Incorrect. Result derived from using distance in kilometers instead of meters.
Incorrect. Factor of $10^3$ error in order of magnitude.
Incorrect. Forgot to square distance $d$ in denominator.

questions.topic: Universal Gravitation - Variation of Weight with Altitude
questions.q: At what altitude $h$ above Earth's surface must one go so that their weight is halved? ($R_T = 6371\text{ km}$, $M_T = 5.972 \cdot 10^{24}\text{ kg}$).
questions.hint: Set the weight at altitude $h$ equal to half the surface weight: $G \frac{M_T m}{(R_T + h)^2} = \frac{1}{2} G \frac{M_T m}{R_T^2}$. Simplifying yields $(R_T + h)^2 = 2 R_T^2 \implies h = (\sqrt{2} - 1) R_T$.
explanations: Correct! Solving for altitude from $(R_T + h) = \sqrt{2} R_T$, we get $h = (\sqrt{2} - 1) R_T \approx 0.4142 \cdot 6371\text{ km} \approx 2639\text{ km} \approx 2630\text{ km}$.
Incorrect. $3185\text{ km}$ simply corresponds to half the Earth's radius $R_T / 2$.
Incorrect. At an altitude equal to Earth's radius $h = R_T$, gravity and weight become $1/4$ of surface weight, not half.
Incorrect. Corresponds to twice Earth's radius.

questions.topic: Universal Gravitation - Earth-Sun Gravitational Equilibrium Point
questions.q: At what distance $x$ from Earth, along the line joining Earth and the Sun, must a space probe be located so that Earth's gravitational pull exactly balances that of the Sun? ($M_T = 5.972 \cdot 10^{24}\text{ kg}$, $M_S = 1.99 \cdot 10^{30}\text{ kg}$, Earth-Sun distance $d = 1.5 \cdot 10^8\text{ km}$).
questions.hint: Equate the two gravitational forces: $G \frac{M_T m}{x^2} = G \frac{M_S m}{(d - x)^2}$. Taking the square root on both sides yields $\frac{\sqrt{M_T}}{x} = \frac{\sqrt{M_S}}{d - x}$, from which $x = \frac{\sqrt{M_T}}{\sqrt{M_S} + \sqrt{M_T}} d$.
explanations: Correct! Calculating mass root ratio: $\frac{\sqrt{M_T}}{\sqrt{M_S}} = \sqrt{\frac{5.972 \cdot 10^{24}}{1.99 \cdot 10^{30}}} \approx 1.732 \cdot 10^{-3}$. Substituting into relation $x \approx 1.732 \cdot 10^{-3} \cdot 1.5 \cdot 10^8\text{ km} \approx 2.6 \cdot 10^5\text{ km}$.
Incorrect. Overestimated value due to error in simplifying mass ratio.
Incorrect. Calculation error in square root of mass ratio $M_T / M_S$.
Incorrect. $7.5 \cdot 10^7\text{ km}$ is the exact midpoint between Earth and Sun.

questions.topic: Universal Gravitation - Acceleration due to Gravity on the Moon
questions.q: Knowing that the mass of the Moon is $M_L = 7.34 \cdot 10^{22}\text{ kg}$ and its radius is $R_L = 1.74 \cdot 10^6\text{ m}$, calculate gravitational acceleration $g_L$ at its surface.
questions.hint: Surface gravitational acceleration is given by formula $g_L = G \frac{M_L}{R_L^2}$, with $G = 6.674 \cdot 10^{-11}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$.
explanations: Correct! Applying formula $g_L = (6.674 \cdot 10^{-11}) \cdot \frac{7.34 \cdot 10^{22}}{(1.74 \cdot 10^6)^2} = \frac{4.8987 \cdot 10^{12}}{3.0276 \cdot 10^{12}} \approx 1.62\text{ m/s}^2$.
Incorrect. $9.81\text{ m/s}^2$ is the average gravitational acceleration on Earth's surface.
Incorrect. Error in calculating the square of lunar radius $R_L$.
Incorrect. Corresponds to approximately half of real lunar gravitational acceleration.

questions.topic: Gravitation and Orbital Dynamics - Binary Star System
questions.q: Plaskett's binary star system consists of a pair of stars of equal mass $M$ in circular orbits around their common center of mass (midpoint of joining line). The orbital speed of each star is $v = 220\text{ km/s}$ and rotation period is $T = 14.4\text{ days}$. Determine mass $M$ of each star.
questions.hint: First calculate orbit radius $r = \frac{v \cdot T}{2\pi}$ (converting $T$ to seconds). Distance between the two stars is $2r$. Equating mutual gravity force to centripetal force: $G \frac{M^2}{(2r)^2} = M \frac{v^2}{r} \implies M = \frac{4 v^2 r}{G}$.
explanations: Correct! Period in seconds is $T = 14.4 \cdot 86400 = 1.24416 \cdot 10^6\text{ s}$. Orbital radius is $r = \frac{220000 \cdot 1.24416 \cdot 10^6}{2\pi} \approx 4.356 \cdot 10^{10}\text{ m}$. From dynamic condition $M = \frac{4 v^2 r}{G} = \frac{4 \cdot (220000)^2 \cdot (4.356 \cdot 10^{10})}{6.674 \cdot 10^{-11}} \approx 1.26 \cdot 10^{32}\text{ kg}$.
Incorrect. Result halved due to error in using distance $2r$ in gravitation equation.
Incorrect. Result doubled due to not dividing correctly by centripetal factor.
Incorrect. Error in converting period from days to seconds.

questions.topic: Kepler's Third Law - Distance of Mars from the Sun
questions.q: The period of revolution of Mars around the Sun is $687\text{ days}$, equal to $1.88\text{ years}$. Determine the distance of Mars from the Sun using the Earth-Sun distance ($1\text{ AU}$) as a reference unit.
questions.hint: Apply Kepler's third law in the form $\frac{T^2}{r^3} = \text{constant}$. Expressing period in years and distance in Astronomical Units ($T_E = 1\text{ year}$, $r_E = 1\text{ AU}$), distance of Mars is obtained as $r_M = (T_M)^{2/3}$.
explanations: Correct! With $T_M = 1.88\text{ years}$, applying Kepler's third law yields $r_M = (1.88)^{2/3} = \sqrt[3]{1.88^2} = \sqrt[3]{3.5344} \approx 1.52\text{ AU}$ (that is, $1.52$ times the Earth-Sun distance).
Incorrect. $2.82$ is obtained by directly squaring the period without taking the cube root.
Incorrect. $3.53$ corresponds to $T_M^2$, i.e. square of orbital period.
Incorrect. Result derived from incorrect calculation of $2/3$ exponent.

questions.topic: Gravitation and Orbital Motion - Period of Orbit around Jupiter
questions.q: A spacecraft is in orbit around Jupiter. The radius of the orbit is $3$ times the radius of the planet ($R_J = 71500\text{ km}$). Knowing that on Jupiter's surface gravitational acceleration is $23\text{ N/kg}$, calculate the orbital period of the spacecraft.
questions.hint: Express the product $G M_J$ via surface gravity: $g_J = \frac{G M_J}{R_J^2} \implies G M_J = g_J R_J^2$. The period of orbit with radius $r = 3 R_J$ is $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{r^3}{G M_J}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{27 R_J}{g_J}}$.
explanations: Correct! Substituting data $R_J = 7.15 \cdot 10^7\text{ m}$ and $g_J = 23\text{ m/s}^2$: $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{27 \cdot 7.15 \cdot 10^7}{23}} = 2\pi \sqrt{8.393 \cdot 10^7} \approx 2\pi \cdot 9161.5 \approx 57564\text{ s}$. Converting to hours: $\frac{57564}{3600} \approx 15.99\text{ hours} \approx 16\text{ hours}$.
Incorrect. $8\text{ hours}$ is obtained if forgetting factor $3^3 = 27$ in numerator under square root.
Incorrect. Overestimated value due to error in converting seconds to hours.
Incorrect. Result derived from improperly doubling orbital time.

questions.topic: Areostationary Satellites - Synchronous Orbit Radius of Mars
questions.q: Mars has a mass of about $6.42 \cdot 10^{23}\text{ kg}$ and completes one full rotation on its axis in $24\text{ h } 37\text{ min}$. At what distance from the center of the planet should an artificial satellite be placed so that it remains stationary above a given point on the surface of Mars?
questions.hint: Convert rotation period to seconds: $T = 24 \cdot 3600 + 37 \cdot 60 = 88620\text{ s}$. Apply synchronous orbit equation $r = \left( \frac{G M T^2}{4\pi^2} \right)^{1/3}$.
explanations: Correct! Substituting $T = 88620\text{ s}$, $M = 6.42 \cdot 10^{23}\text{ kg}$, and $G = 6.674 \cdot 10^{-11}$: $r^3 = \frac{(6.674 \cdot 10^{-11}) \cdot (6.42 \cdot 10^{23}) \cdot (88620)^2}{4\pi^2} \approx 8.516 \cdot 10^{21}\text{ m}^3$. Taking cube root: $r = \sqrt[3]{8.516 \cdot 10^{21}} \approx 2.042 \cdot 10^7\text{ m} = 2.04 \cdot 10^7\text{ m}$.
Incorrect. $4.22 \cdot 10^7\text{ m}$ is geostationary orbit radius around Earth.
Incorrect. Result due to failing to square period $T$.
Incorrect. Value of $r^3$ before taking cube root.

questions.topic: Escape Velocity - Planet Mars
questions.q: Determine the escape velocity needed to escape the gravity of planet Mars, knowing that its radius is $3430\text{ km}$ and its mass is $6.37 \cdot 10^{23}\text{ kg}$.
questions.hint: Use the escape velocity formula $v_{escape} = \sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R}}$. Remember to express radius in meters: $R = 3.43 \cdot 10^6\text{ m}$.
explanations: Correct! Calculating $v_{escape} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \cdot (6.674 \cdot 10^{-11}) \cdot (6.37 \cdot 10^{23})}{3.43 \cdot 10^6}} = \sqrt{24785830} \approx 4978.5\text{ m/s} \approx 4977\text{ m/s} = 4.98\text{ km/s}$.
Incorrect. $11.2\text{ km/s}$ is the escape velocity from Earth's surface.
Incorrect. $2.38\text{ km/s}$ is the escape velocity from the Moon's surface.
Incorrect. Result derived from missing factor $2$ inside square root ($v_{orb}$).

questions.topic: Escape Velocity - In terms of Surface Acceleration
questions.q: A planet of radius $R = 6.0 \cdot 10^7\text{ m}$ has a surface gravitational field of intensity $g = 30\text{ m/s}^2$. What is the escape velocity from the planet?
questions.hint: Recalling that $g = \frac{G M}{R^2}$, we can substitute $G M = g R^2$ into the escape velocity equation to get $v_{escape} = \sqrt{2 g R}$.
explanations: Correct! Applying $v_{escape} = \sqrt{2 g R} = \sqrt{2 \cdot 30 \cdot (6.0 \cdot 10^7)} = \sqrt{3.6 \cdot 10^9} = \sqrt{3600 \cdot 10^6} = 60000\text{ m/s} = 60\text{ km/s}$.
Incorrect. $30\text{ km/s}$ is obtained if forgetting to multiply by $2$ under the square root.
Incorrect. Doubled result due to calculation error.
Incorrect. Result due to incorrect square root of $3.6 \cdot 10^9$.

questions.topic: Conservation of Energy - Vertical Launch and Maximum Distance
questions.q: A body is launched perpendicularly to the Earth's surface with a speed equal to half the escape velocity ($v = \frac{1}{2} v_{escape}$). At what maximum distance $r_{max}$ from the center of Earth does it stop? (Neglect friction).
questions.hint: Use conservation of mechanical energy: $E_i = \frac{1}{2}m v^2 - \frac{G M m}{R_T}$. Since $v^2 = \frac{1}{4} v_{escape}^2 = \frac{1}{4} \left(\frac{2 G M}{R_T}\right) = \frac{G M}{2 R_T}$, we get $E_i = -\frac{3}{4} \frac{G M m}{R_T}$. At the maximum distance point $v=0$, so $E_f = -\frac{G M m}{r_{max}}$.
explanations: Correct! Equating initial and final energy: $-\frac{3}{4} \frac{G M m}{R_T} = -\frac{G M m}{r_{max}} \implies r_{max} = \frac{4}{3} R_T$ (meaning an altitude $h = \frac{1}{3} R_T$ above the surface).
Incorrect. $2 R_T$ would be erroneously obtained assuming a uniform gravitational field.
Incorrect. $3/2 R_T$ stems from an error in initial kinetic energy balance.
Incorrect. Result derived from incorrectly inverting the fraction $3/4$.

questions.topic: Work and Kinetic Energy - Car Acceleration
questions.q: Calculate the work $L$ done by the engine of a car of mass $m = 700\text{ kg}$ to increase its speed from $0$ to $90\text{ km/h}$ (neglecting friction). Furthermore, determine to what fraction of the original kinetic energy the kinetic energy is reduced if the speed is halved.
questions.hint: Convert speed to $\text{m/s}$ ($90\text{ km/h} = 25\text{ m/s}$). Apply work-energy theorem $L = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}m v_f^2$.
options: $L \approx 2.2 \cdot 10^5\text{ J}$ and kinetic energy reduces to $1/4$
$L \approx 4.4 \cdot 10^5\text{ J}$ and kinetic energy reduces to $1/2$
$L \approx 2.2 \cdot 10^5\text{ J}$ and kinetic energy reduces to $1/8$
$L \approx 1.1 \cdot 10^5\text{ J}$ and kinetic energy reduces to $1/4$
explanations: Correct! Converting $v_f = 25\text{ m/s}$, work is $L = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 700 \cdot 25^2 = 218750\text{ J} \approx 2.2 \cdot 10^5\text{ J}$. If speed halves ($v' = v/2$), kinetic energy becomes $K' = \frac{1}{2}m (v/2)^2 = \frac{1}{4} (\frac{1}{2}m v^2) = \frac{1}{4} K$, reducing to $1/4$ of the original value.
Incorrect. $4.4 \cdot 10^5\text{ J}$ is obtained if forgetting to divide by $2$ in kinetic energy formula.
Incorrect. Kinetic energy varies with the square of speed ($1/2^2 = 1/4$), not cube ($1/8$).
Incorrect. $1.1 \cdot 10^5\text{ J}$ is obtained by incorrectly using $v = 25/2\text{ m/s}$ in initial work calculation.

questions.topic: Work-Energy Theorem - Calculating Final Speed
questions.q: A force doing work $L = 4\text{ J}$ is applied to a body of mass $m = 500\text{ g}$. If the body was initially moving with speed $v_i = 3\text{ m/s}$, calculate its final speed $v_f$.
questions.hint: Convert mass to kilograms ($m = 0.5\text{ kg}$). Use the work-energy theorem $L = \frac{1}{2}m v_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}m v_i^2$ and solve for $v_f$.
explanations: Correct! Initial kinetic energy is $K_i = \frac{1}{2} (0.5) (3^2) = 2.25\text{ J}$. From work theorem $L = K_f - K_i \implies 4 = \frac{1}{2}(0.5) v_f^2 - 2.25 \implies 0.25 v_f^2 = 6.25 \implies v_f^2 = 25 \implies v_f = 5\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. Result derived from an error in adding work to initial kinetic energy.
Incorrect. $25$ is the squared speed value $v_f^2$, forgetting to take the square root.
Incorrect. Calculation error in converting grams to kilograms.

questions.topic: Work-Energy Theorem - Braking Force
questions.q: A body of mass $m = 90\text{ kg}$ moving at $10\text{ m/s}$ reduces its speed to $3\text{ m/s}$ during $40\text{ m}$ of braking. Calculate the magnitude of the average braking force $F$ acting on it.
questions.hint: The work done by braking force is $L = -F \cdot s$. By the work-energy theorem, $L = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}m (v_f^2 - v_i^2)$.
explanations: Correct! The change in kinetic energy is $\Delta K = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 90 \cdot (3^2 - 10^2) = 45 \cdot (9 - 100) = -4095\text{ J}$. Since $L = -F \cdot s = -4095\text{ J}$, we have $F = \frac{4095}{40} = 102.375\text{ N} \approx 100\text{ N}$.
Incorrect. Result doubled due to calculation error in factor $1/2$.
Incorrect. $410\text{ N}$ is obtained if forgetting to divide by braking distance $s = 40\text{ m}$.
Incorrect. Results from considering speed change $(10 - 3)$ instead of change in squared speeds.

questions.topic: Kinetic Energy and Explosive Equivalent - Locomotive Collision
questions.q: Two locomotives of mass $m = 120 \cdot 10^3\text{ kg}$ each are initially separated by a distance $d = 6.4\text{ km}$ and start moving directly toward each other with constant acceleration $a = 0.26\text{ m/s}^2$. Calculate total kinetic energy at impact and TNT equivalent mass required to produce the same energy, knowing that $1\text{ t}$ ($1000\text{ kg}$) of TNT yields $4.18 \cdot 10^9\text{ J}$.
questions.hint: The locomotives collide at midpoint $s = d/2 = 3200\text{ m}$. Speed of each at impact satisfies $v^2 = 2 a s$. Total kinetic energy is $K_{tot} = 2 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2} m v^2\right) = m (2 a s)$. Substitute values to find $K_{tot}$ and divide by TNT specific energy ($4.18 \cdot 10^6\text{ J/kg}$).
explanations: Correct! Each locomotive travels $s = 3200\text{ m}$, so $v^2 = 2 \cdot 0.26 \cdot 3200 = 1664\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$. Kinetic energy of a single locomotive is $K_1 = \frac{1}{2} (120000) (1664) \approx 10^8\text{ J}$, and total energy is $K_{tot} = 2 K_1 = 1.9968 \cdot 10^8\text{ J} \approx 2 \cdot 10^8\text{ J}$. Dividing by the energy of $1\text{ kg}$ of TNT ($4.18 \cdot 10^6\text{ J}$): $M_{TNT} = \frac{1.9968 \cdot 10^8}{4.18 \cdot 10^6} \approx 47.8\text{ kg} \approx 48\text{ kg}$.
Incorrect. $1 \cdot 10^8\text{ J}$ and $24\text{ kg}$ are calculated considering kinetic energy of only one locomotive instead of both.
Incorrect. Result doubled for considering the entire distance $6.4\text{ km}$ for each locomotive instead of $3.2\text{ km}$.
Incorrect. Factor of $10$ error in converting tons to kilograms of TNT.

questions.topic: Proton Kinematics and Work - Final Velocity in Linear Accelerator
questions.q: A proton ($m = 1.67 \cdot 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$) enters a stage of a linear accelerator of length $d = 3.5\text{ cm}$ with initial speed $v_i = 2.7 \cdot 10^7\text{ m/s}$. Undergoing constant acceleration $a = 3.6 \cdot 10^{15}\text{ m/s}^2$, calculate its exit speed $v_f$ from the stage.
questions.hint: Convert length to meters ($d = 0.035\text{ m}$). Use kinematic equation $v_f^2 = v_i^2 + 2 a d$.
explanations: Correct! Converting $d = 0.035\text{ m}$, $v_f^2 = (2.7 \cdot 10^7)^2 + 2 \cdot (3.6 \cdot 10^{15}) \cdot 0.035 = 7.29 \cdot 10^{14} + 2.52 \cdot 10^{14} = 9.81 \cdot 10^{14}\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$. Taking square root: $v_f = \sqrt{9.81 \cdot 10^{14}} \approx 3.13 \cdot 10^7\text{ m/s} \approx 3.1 \cdot 10^7\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. Result doubled due to error in calculating square root.
Incorrect. Results from forgetting factor $2$ in the $2 a d$ term.
Incorrect. $9.8 \cdot 10^{14}$ is the value of squared speed $v_f^2$ in $\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$.

questions.topic: Proton Kinematics and Work - Kinetic Energy Gain
questions.q: A proton of mass $m = 1.67 \cdot 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$ accelerates at $a = 3.6 \cdot 10^{15}\text{ m/s}^2$ over a distance $d = 3.5\text{ cm}$, increasing its speed from $v_i = 2.7 \cdot 10^7\text{ m/s}$ to $v_f \approx 3.1 \cdot 10^7\text{ m/s}$. Find the gain in kinetic energy $\Delta K$ achieved during this acceleration.
questions.hint: The kinetic energy gain equals the work done by the force: $\Delta K = L = F \cdot d = m a d$, or the difference between final and initial kinetic energies $\Delta K = \frac{1}{2}m (v_f^2 - v_i^2)$.
explanations: Correct! Using rounded velocity values $v_f = 3.1 \cdot 10^7\text{ m/s}$ and $v_i = 2.7 \cdot 10^7\text{ m/s}$, we get $\Delta K = \frac{1}{2} (1.67 \cdot 10^{-27}) \cdot [(3.1 \cdot 10^7)^2 - (2.7 \cdot 10^7)^2] = 0.835 \cdot 10^{-27} \cdot (9.61 - 7.29) \cdot 10^{14} \approx 1.937 \cdot 10^{-13}\text{ J} \approx 1.9 \cdot 10^{-13}\text{ J}$ (the unrounded exact value $m a d$ is $2.1 \cdot 10^{-13}\text{ J}$).
Incorrect. Result doubled due to missing division by $2$.
Incorrect. Order of magnitude error from using $d = 3.5$ instead of $d = 0.035\text{ m}$.
Incorrect. Error in calculating the squared difference of speeds.
